name: Superior cervical ganglion
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: The largest and most cephalad ganglion of the sympathetic trunk, lying behind the internal carotid artery at the C1-C2 level. Receives preganglionic fibers that have ascended from the upper thoracic cord without synapsing; every postganglionic fiber reaching the head originates here.

name: Superior cervical ganglion
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Internal carotid nerve
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Ascends with the internal carotid artery into its own sympathetic plexus around the vessel; this is the sole route by which sympathetic fibers reach the orbit and cranial cavity, which is why a lesion anywhere along the chain below this point (a Pancoast tumor, carotid dissection, or a stellate ganglion block) produces the same ipsilateral Horner's triad.
targets: cavernous plexus around the internal carotid artery, dilator pupillae and superior tarsal (Muller's) muscles via the ciliary ganglion and long ciliary nerves, and sweat glands of the forehead following the ophthalmic artery -- interruption here produces Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)

name: Middle cervical ganglion
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: The smallest and most inconstant cervical ganglion (absent or fused with its neighbors in a substantial minority of people), at the level of the cricoid cartilage near the inferior thyroid artery. Contributes to the cardiac plexus and to the thyroid gland's sympathetic supply.

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion
root_contributions: C8-T1 (fused inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglia)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Bhatia A, Flamer D, Peng PWH, Reg Anesth Pain Med 37:12 (2012) [stellate ganglion block technique]
notes: Lies anterior to the C7 transverse process and the neck of the first rib, just posterior to the vertebral artery's origin -- the reason ultrasound guidance (targeting the C6 tubercle or C7 level, avoiding the vertebral artery) has largely replaced the blind anterior paratracheal approach for stellate ganglion block, used for complex regional pain syndrome of the upper limb, refractory angina, and some vascular insufficiency syndromes. A successful block reproduces Horner's syndrome, which is the clinical proof the block reached its target rather than evidence of a complication.

name: Thoracic sympathetic chain
root_contributions: T1-T12 (12 paravertebral ganglia, modeled as one chain entry)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Runs along the heads of the ribs, deep to the parietal pleura -- a thoracic sympathectomy or splanchnic nerve block risks the pleura directly. Upper ganglia (T2-T4) supply the upper limb and are the target of endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy for palmar hyperhidrosis; the lower ganglia (T5-T12) give rise to the splanchnic nerves.

name: Greater splanchnic nerve
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Pierces the diaphragmatic crus to reach the abdomen, carrying preganglionic fibers that do not synapse until the celiac ganglion -- this is why splanchnic and celiac plexus neurolysis (for pancreatic cancer pain) target the same functional pathway from two different levels.

name: Greater splanchnic nerve
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

targets: celiac ganglion and plexus (preganglionic fibers relay here before reaching stomach, liver, spleen, and pancreas) -- converges with the right greater splanchnic nerve and both vagal trunks, modeled here as a single convergence point rather than multiple tree parents

name: Lesser splanchnic nerve
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
targets: aorticorenal ganglion (preganglionic relay for the kidney and adrenal medulla)

name: Lesser splanchnic nerve
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Least (lowest) splanchnic nerve
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Present in roughly half of people; when absent its fibers travel with the lesser splanchnic nerve.

name: Lumbar sympathetic chain
root_contributions: L1-L5 (typically 4 paravertebral ganglia, modeled as one chain entry)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Nebab EG, Florence IM, Anesth Analg 95:1687 (2002) [lumbar sympathetic block technique]
notes: Runs along the anterolateral border of the vertebral bodies, medial to psoas major -- the needle path for a lumbar sympathetic block passes through or just anterior to psoas, which is what separates this block from a psoas compartment (lumbar plexus) block done from the same posterior approach at a similar depth. Used for lower-limb complex regional pain syndrome, phantom limb pain, and lower-limb vascular insufficiency, mirroring the stellate ganglion's role for the upper limb.

name: Sacral sympathetic chain
root_contributions: S1-S4 (typically 4-5 paravertebral ganglia, modeled as one chain entry)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Runs on the anterior sacral surface medial to the sacral foramina, converging with its opposite-side chain at the ganglion impar in front of the coccyx.

name: Sacral sympathetic chain
root_contributions: S1-S4 (typically 4-5 paravertebral ganglia, modeled as one chain entry)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Ganglion impar (of Walther)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Oh CS et al., Reg Anesth Pain Med 29:270 (2004) [ganglion impar block technique]
notes: The single midline terminus where both sacral sympathetic chains fuse, anterior to the sacrococcygeal joint. Modeled here as a child of the right chain alone; it is anatomically the meeting point of both. Its block (transsacrococcygeal or paracoccygeal approach) treats coccydynia and other sympathetically mediated perineal/anorectal pain, and is one of the few midline neuraxial-adjacent targets reached from directly behind the coccyx.
targets: sympathetic and visceral afferent fibers to the coccyx, perineum, distal rectum, and anus -- a terminal midline relay, not a named end-organ

name: Celiac plexus (solar plexus)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Malfertheiner P et al. (celiac plexus neurolysis literature, general reference)
notes: The largest prevertebral autonomic plexus, surrounding the celiac trunk's origin from the aorta at approximately T12-L1, flanked by the paired celiac ganglia. Receives the greater and lesser splanchnic nerves bilaterally and both vagal trunks -- modeled here as a child of the right greater splanchnic nerve alone as a tree-structure simplification. Celiac plexus block/neurolysis (percutaneous retrocrural, anterior transabdominal, or endoscopic-ultrasound-guided) treats pain from pancreatic and other upper-abdominal malignancy by interrupting visceral afferents before they reach the cord.
targets: stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, and small and large bowel to the splenic flexure -- essentially all foregut and midgut viscera, via the subsidiary hepatic, splenic, superior mesenteric and renal plexuses

name: Superior hypogastric plexus
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Plancarte R et al., Anesthesiology 73:236 (1990) [superior hypogastric plexus block technique]
notes: Lies anterior to the L5-S1 disc and sacral promontory, continuing the aortic plexus inferiorly before dividing into the two hypogastric nerves that carry sympathetic (and mixed) fibers down to the pelvic (inferior hypogastric) plexuses. Its block treats pelvic cancer pain and some chronic pelvic pain syndromes, approached posterolaterally at the L4-L5 level to reach anterior to the sacral promontory.

name: Inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Lies against the lateral pelvic wall alongside the internal iliac vessels, receiving sympathetic input from the hypogastric nerve and parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) in the same plexus -- one of the few points in the body where sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers share a single named plexus before diverging to their end organs.
targets: bladder, rectum, and (uterus and vagina, or prostate and seminal vesicles) via the vesical, middle/inferior rectal, and uterovaginal or prostatic nerve subplexuses; also the corpora cavernosa/clitoris via the cavernous nerves, making this plexus the anatomical basis of pelvic organ and erectile innervation
